pinboard.description:
Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task.

Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer — the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer — likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers.

So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer.

“It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect.

pinboard.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
pinboard.description:
We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.

Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting, a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.
Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases

Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.

Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

    Active (wake) phase: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
    Sleep phase: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.

While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.
Key components of the sleep process

The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.

Anthropic illegally trained Claude with Stanford professors’ books
pinboard.description:
The AI company pirated at least 10 Stanford academics’ work in a $1.5 billion copyright settlement.

AI giant Anthropic illegally scraped and pirated the work of over 10 Stanford professors to train its Claude models, a federal judge ruled in a May 2026 lawsuit.

Anthropic previously trained Claude on illegally obtained texts from professors Tobias Wolff, Abraham Verghese, Chang-Rae Lee, Daniel Mason, Hayagreeva Rao and Myra Strober. In Bartz v. Anthropic, which the Authors Alliance calls the largest copyright settlement involving an AI company, Judge William Alsup ruled that Anthropic could no longer pirate books to create a permanent central library.

While blocking the piracy of work to train AI, Alsup justified the legal acquisition of books to train Claude’s Large Language Models (LLMs) as fair use. He compared AI training to how humans can read, internalize and remember a book’s themes and style. “Like any reader aspiring to be a writer, Anthropic’s LLMs trained upon works not to race ahead and replicate or supplant them — but to turn a hard corner and create something different,” he wrote.

The $1.5 billion settlement went to authors and publishers of nearly 500,000 registered works. Wolff and 27 other authors say the settlement isn’t enough.

“To put me to work that way, without remittance, is a form of slave labor,” said Wolff, professor emeritus of English and winner of the National Medal of Arts. “They’re using my work without paying for it. As time goes on, they’re going to make the lives of writers very difficult if there’s no fruit to their labor.”  

10 of Wolff’s publications had been used for AI training without permission. 

“[The settlement] still gives Anthropic pretty free rein to roam through our literature and basically take what they think will be useful and profitable for them,” Wolff said. 

Wolff, along with English professor Chang-rae Lee, opted out of the Bartz settlement. In May 2026, they filed the separate non-class lawsuit Cruz v. Anthropic, seeking a jury trial for full statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work, surpassing the approximate $3,000 of damages per work offered in the Bartz settlement.

Similar to the claims in Bartz, the plaintiffs allege that Anthropic illegally downloaded, reproduced and distributed their copyrighted books from “shadow libraries” like LibGen and PiLiMi, and that Anthropic broke the law by downloading and storing the pirated files in a central library. 

“Our agents didn’t think the blanket lawsuit covered quite enough of the liability to us and are seeking redress in more particular ways,” Wolff said. 

If Wolff and his fellow authors are successful, they would gain a permanent injunction against Claude model training using their works. 

Paul Goldstein, a Stanford Law leading scholar in intellectual property and one of the plaintiffs represented in the class action, acknowledged the difficulty of addressing and preventing copyright issues for AI companies. 

“The essential problem … is what economists call ‘transaction costs,’” Goldstein wrote in an email

Reproducing civilization - by Joseph Heath - In Due Course
pinboard.description: Human civilization is built on institutional kluges. Indeed, a civilization can be defined as a society that possesses an institutional structure that extends cooperation beyond the scope of what its members could sustain through their onboard behavioural dispositions and proclivities. This is why they are always in danger of fragmenting into smaller-scale but psychologically more intuitive social formations. This is also why civilizations must be actively defended, first and foremost against the large segments of their own populations who have never really bought into these arrangements. The lack of public buy-in is particularly easy to demonstrate in the case of liberal democracy, where it has long been known that these systems are not sustained by the prevalence of either liberal or democratic values in the public at large. (The fact that democratic institutions are essentially imposed upon the people by elites was referred to, famously, by Thomas Dye and Harmon Ziegler as The Irony of Democracy.) To the extent that the system is successfully reproduced, it is by retaining the allegiance of these elites.
